messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Kian was twenty-four, the relationship he had built his life around ended not with a conversation, but with a violent lunge in their apartment hallway. His former partner pinned him against the peeling paint, his knuckles striking Kian’s ribs with practiced force before whispering threats into his ear. The violence was sudden, physical, and deeply violating. In the months that followed, the event refused to settle into a distant past. Instead, the memory arrived with jarring immediacy, overwriting his current surroundings until he felt the exact ache in his bruised ribs and the crushing grip on his shoulders. The emotional surge was so paralyzing that he would have to stop mid-sentence, pressing his palms flat against his desk to ground himself. This relentless reliving convinced him of a quiet truth: he was inadequate, and people could never truly be trusted. Because he came to believe he was inherently weak, the world quickly transformed into a landscape of unpredictable danger. As a twenty-seven-year-old South Eastern Asian American journalist, Kian’s assignment desk required long commutes across the city. Riding the municipal bus became a daily test of endurance. The moment the doors closed and the vehicle lurched into traffic, the proximity of other passengers, particularly men, would spike his pulse. To manage that sudden alarm, he developed rigid habits: he never allowed himself to feel or express the anger bubbling in his chest, simply swallowing it down, and he began skipping lunch to avoid the vulnerability of sitting in crowded cafeterias. These suppressions kept his professional facade intact, but they slowly starved him of the energy to process what had happened. His deep-seated fear of harm guided these retreats, convincing him that avoiding public transit and elevators with male colleagues was the only viable shield. Each time he navigated the crowded newsroom or waited for an elevator, the triggers would flood back unbidden. The sensory overload of the city dragged him directly into the hallway attack, his breath hitching at the familiar scent of leather and stale coffee that mimicked his ex’s cologne. Once the memory took hold, it dictated his movements; he found himself scanning every room for exits, his attention fixated on any male presence, because the past felt so immediate that he had to treat every moment like a prelude to another assault. Because he had come to believe that harm was always imminent, ordinary delays in his work took on a sinister weight. When a source failed to return an email or a deadline stretched longer than expected, he would assume the worst was already in motion, jumping to conclusions that he was being set up. This constant anticipation of catastrophe meant he could not trust safety, even when his editor assured him the newsroom was secure. The sheer exhaustion of this vigilance eventually whispered to him that his own judgment was fundamentally flawed, cementing his sense of inadequacy. By consistently silencing his anger and rationalizing his avoidance as prudence, he fed the narrative that he lacked the agency to change his circumstances. As winter approached, the cycle tightened into a relentless pattern. Every time he rode the bus to a source meeting, the memory would overwrite the present, dragging him into the physical sensation of being cornered. The reliving of the event convinced him that he was inadequate and that danger was an inescapable reality. This conviction made delays feel like imminent threats, which in turn forced him to avoid male colleagues and crowded transit. The avoidance kept him safe for an hour, but it also starved him of the support he desperately needed, reinforcing his belief that he could never trust anyone. The loop pulled him tighter each day, leaving him physically exhausted and emotionally stranded. His editor eventually had to reassign his beat, noting that his chronic fatigue and erratic attendance had compromised his reporting deadlines, a professional setback that confirmed his innermost fears. Now, Kian sits in a therapist’s office, his hands wrapped tightly around a cold cup of coffee. What finally brought him here was a panic attack during a live editorial meeting, where the sudden noise of phones ringing triggered the same chest pain he felt years ago, leaving him unable to speak or breathe for three full minutes. He is afraid that the memories will never lose their edge, that he will always be walking through a world that feels ready to collapse into violence. What he hopes for, quietly and desperately, is to find a way to separate the past from the present, to stop bracing for blows that are no longer coming, and to finally believe that he is safe enough to simply live, even while maintaining the relationship that currently steadies his days.
